title: The Butterfly
full_review:
A neglected child who's never seen the countryside hides in her crusty old neighbor's car as he embarks on a trip from Paris to the Alps in the French charmer "The Butterfly" (First Run).

Septuagenarian Julien (Michel Serrault) lives alone in his Paris apartment -- if you don't count one room filled with plants and live butterflies. Into the building moves 8-year-old Elsa (Claire Bouanich) and her single mom, who works such long hours Elsa is often left to her own devices.

Seeing the child left outside without her key one day, Julien rather reluctantly invites her into his apartment, where she is fascinated by his framed butterfly collection. Leaving for a few minutes, he warns her not to go in his greenhouse room, but of course she does and he returns to find his precious butterflies taking flight. Elsa is banished.

Julien embarks on a 10-day trip to capture a rare butterfly, the Isabella, which lives only three days and three nights in the mountains. At first day's end he is angered to find stowaway Elsa in his car, but the child's pleadings that she has never been outside the city and so wants to travel with him wear down his better judgment and they continue on.

No little angel, Elsa gives him the number of a corner phone booth instead of her mother's and later disables his cell phone so he cannot assure her mother she is with him and OK. Understandably, the police consider Elsa's disappearance a kidnapping. But this weaker story line is wisely underplayed.

Viewers should be enthralled by the exquisitely handled discovery of nature through a child's eyes. Dappled meadows and hillsides that glow a lime green in the sunlight are visually intoxicating, but this is no mere travelogue from writer-director Philippe Muyl. The developing relationship between the old man and the wonder-filled child is realistically presented with its several ups and downs, but is never awash in sentimentality. What they find together is much more than an exotic butterfly. And when the trip is over (and not without some needless melodrama), Julien is able to gently advise Elsa's mom she must make time to frequently tell the vulnerable child "I love you."

Young Bouanich is almost too cute for her own good with her auburn locks and a dusting of freckles across her nose and cheeks, but her spunkiness comes through endearingly. Veteran Serrault is also convincing as the outwardly foreboding but eventually tenderhearted caretaker, and there are enough plot developments along their journey to reveal what his life has been and why he seeks to capture this one special butterfly.

One highlight is when Julien entertains Elsa one evening by creating animal silhouettes behind a sheet with his hands, speaking of life and death in a film that is very pro-life whether it lasts into old age or just the life span of an Isabella.

Child, mother and grandfather figure all are transformed in heartening ways by the film's conclusion. Offering considerable emotional satisfaction, this gloriously shot and beautifully told tale of bonding transcends the formula of an innocent child melting the heart of a confirmed curmudgeon. The metamorphosis from ugly pupa to cocoon to winged butterfly is apt for a richly textured, very human film that slowly but very skillfully takes flight. Subtitles. Due to brief sexual references and occasional profanity, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. Not rated by the Motion Picture Association of America.
